claim: The Bevel tool/modifier's Harden Normals option assigns custom split normals to the newly created bevel faces so they appear smoothly shaded without affecting the shading of the rest of the mesh -- this is distinct from and complementary to the mesh-wide Smooth-by-Angle shading policy already in use, since Harden Normals only touches the bevel's own new geometry rather than the whole object.
supporting_evidence: Official Blender manual (bundled RST, read 2026-08-14 via mcp__Blender__search_manual_docs): manual/modeling/meshes/editing/edge/bevel.rst, 'Options' section -- 'Harden Normals: When enabled, assigns custom split normals to the newly created faces to make them appear smoothly shaded ... without affecting the rest of the mesh.'

claim: The Bevel tool's Clamp Overlap option prevents beveled edges from overshooting past the end of their neighboring faces -- without it, a bevel whose width grows large enough to reach a neighboring edge/face boundary will overshoot and produce overlapping/self-intersecting geometry instead of stopping cleanly at the collision point.
supporting_evidence: Official Blender manual: manual/modeling/meshes/editing/edge/bevel.rst -- 'Clamp Overlap: Prevents beveled edges from overshooting past the end of their neighboring faces.'

claim: When three or more edges beveled at once meet at a shared vertex, the Miter Outer/Inner settings control whether extra geometry (a 'patch' or 'arc') is generated at that corner to avoid pinching. Outer Miter applies when the corner is more than 180 degrees on the face side (a convex/outer corner); Inner Miter applies when it's less than 180 degrees (a concave/inner corner). Leaving both on 'Sharp' (no extra geometry) risks a pinched/degenerate corner exactly at multi-edge bevel intersections -- a real, named cause for the kind of pinch-candidate defects this project's own diagnostics already look for.
supporting_evidence: Official Blender manual: manual/modeling/meshes/editing/edge/bevel.rst -- 'Miter Outer: ... determines if any extra geometry is created in that corner to avoid pinching' and '(Miter) Inner: ... determines if any extra geometry is created in those corners', both illustrated with sharp/patch/arc comparison images.
rejected_alternative: Leaving Miter Outer/Inner on Sharp (no extra corner geometry) by default at any multi-edge bevel intersection
reason: The manual explicitly frames the non-Sharp miter options as existing specifically to avoid pinching at multi-edge bevel corners -- exactly the kind of surface defect this project's own pinch-candidate diagnostics are built to catch, so this is a documented root cause/fix pair worth knowing before diagnosing a pinch as something else.

claim: The Bevel tool's Face Strength setting (None/New/Affected/All) tags new and/or neighboring faces with a Weak/Medium/Strong strength value, which is meaningless on its own but is consumed by the Weighted Normal modifier's 'Face Influence' option: when Face Influence is enabled, at any vertex where faces of different strength meet, ONLY the normal from the highest-strength face is used for that vertex's final shading normal -- weaker faces are ignored entirely at that vertex, not blended in.
supporting_evidence: Official Blender manual: manual/modeling/meshes/editing/edge/bevel.rst ('Face Strength: ... used in conjunction with a Weight Normals Modifier (with the Face Influence option checked)') cross-referenced with manual/modeling/modifiers/normals/weighted_normal.rst ('Face Influence: ... For example, if three faces meet at a vertex and have the face weights weak, medium, and strong, then only the normal associated with the strong face will be used to set the final result.').
rejected_alternative: Assuming the Weighted Normal modifier always blends/averages all adjacent face normals regardless of any Face Strength tagging
reason: This project has a standing 'bevel-weight policy' for new hard-surface assets; understanding that Face Influence picks the SINGLE strongest face's normal (winner-take-all, not a blend) at each vertex, rather than an averaged result, is the actual mechanism that policy relies on and is worth confirming the project's own bevel-weight workflow is using correctly.

claim: Bridge Edge Loops has a 'Twist' parameter that offsets which target-loop vertex each source-loop vertex connects to. A wrong offset can create a visibly crossed or twisted tube, so loop correspondence must be inspected instead of judging success from face creation alone.
supporting_evidence: Official Blender manual: manual/modeling/meshes/editing/edge/bridge_edge_loops.rst -- 'Twist: Offsets the choice of target vertex which each source vertex is connected to. This makes the generated tube twist along its axis.' Controlled Blender 5.2 evidence in runs/2026-08-15_bridge-correspondence-control/ deliberately applies bad nonzero offsets to equal-density circle and rounded-rectangle loops, reproduces crossed/pinched tubes, then corrects both through the typed runtime and independent verifier.
rejected_alternative: Assuming bridge_selection's lack of a twist/correspondence parameter meant Blender's bridge operation always resolves the 'correct' loop correspondence automatically
reason: The official parameter semantics and two controlled shape transfers establish the narrow mechanism. They do not prove that minimum connector length captures semantic artist intent, and they do not validate the earlier unequal-density teapot connection.

transfer_tests.boundary: controlled equal-density loop correspondence; not held-out prop validation

claim: A practical community workaround for Bridge Edge Loops producing twisted/crossed faces (beyond manually tuning the Twist value, which the manual confirms controls vertex correspondence): select BOTH end faces (not just their boundary edge loops), run Inset Faces, then run Bridge Edge Loops on the resulting inset boundary loops -- this reportedly avoids needing to manually hunt for the correct twist offset. Separately, forum discussion of one specific twisted-bridge case found the fix was simply resetting an accidentally-nonzero Twist value back to 0, confirming Twist is the parameter actually responsible when a bridge comes out visibly rotated/crossed.
supporting_evidence: Blender Artists community forum thread (fetched 2026-08-14), 'Bridge Edge Loops makes twisted faces': a community member identified the reporter's Twist value was set to -36 instead of 0 as the cause; a separate reply suggested insetting both end faces first, then bridging, as a workaround that avoids manual twist-hunting.
rejected_alternative: Manually adjusting the Twist value by trial and error until the bridge looks untwisted, with no starting hypothesis for which value to try
reason: Forum-sourced, lower-confidence than the official manual entry above (0.4 vs 0.55) since it's a single community thread reporting one person's specific case, not authoritative documentation -- worth trying but not yet verified against this project's own mismatched-loop-size scenario (10 vs 12 verts), which is a different situation than the reported case (same vertex count, just a bad twist offset).
